# Srqt in 2026: why scholars still care

Names are not only data points; they ​are cultural evidence. **Srqt** shows why an ASCII spelling can still demand serious scholarship. The sources distinguish this name from every neighboring form, and the temple records that ‌distinction without adding marks the evidence does not contain. What follows is the full picture — name, script, sound, myth, cult, and legacy — ending with the digital home ‌that makes the record easy to reach.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Srqt
- **ASCII form:** serket
- **Meaning:** "She who causes the throat to breathe"
- **Domain of influence:** Scorpions, Healing, ​Poison
- **Pantheon:** Egyptian
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** 𓊃𓂋𓈎𓏏𓁐 (Hieroglyphs)

## Overview

**Srqt** (*serket*) — Scorpions, Poison, Protection of the Vulnerable · She who causes the throat to breathe ​— belongs to the Egyptian tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Scorpions, Healing, Poison". The name means "She who causes the throat to breathe".

**Srqt** — Serket ​— is the scorpion’s sting turned to medicine: the goddess of venom and its cure. She guards the vulnerable — children, the poisoned, the dead in their most ​helpless passage — and her scorpion crawls at the feet of kings and coffins alike, holding the poison at bay by its mere presence.

The name is attested ​in Hieroglyphs as **𓊃𓂋𓈎𓏏𓁐**. Etymologically it means "She who causes the throat to breathe".

The canonical spelling **Srqt** matches the conventional scholarly romanization. The plain ASCII form *serket* contains ​the same letters, so no lost diacritics or encoding transition is claimed. ## The Original ‌Script

The name is preserved in Hieroglyphs as **𓊃𓂋𓈎𓏏𓁐** — Egyptian hieroglyphs, attested Egyptian hieroglyphic, c. 3200 BCE – 4th century CE, in Nile Valley, Egypt. The script ​is written right-to-left / top-to-bottom / multidirectional.

The scholarly transliteration is *Srqt* (Egyptological transliteration), giving the normalized reading Original vocalisation unknown; Egyptological /ˈsɜːr.kɛt/..

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- ‌Hieroglyphic spelling 𓊃𓂋𓈎𓏏𓁐 generated from MdC z:r-q:t-B1
- Read in scholarly transliteration as Srqt
- She who causes the throat to breathe

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈsɜːrkɛt/ ​(conventional)** — Conventional reading — Egyptian vocalisation not attested.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Sr-** — Written srqt; the name is usually explained as “she who causes the throat to ​breathe” (s + rḳ + t).
- **-q-t** — Conventionally vocalised “Serket”; the q is a voiceless uvular stop.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: “SAIR-ket”

Kindred and ​historical forms of the name:

- **Greek** — Σελκίς (Selkís)

Her name is a sentence: the scorpion-goddess as the one who lets the poisoned throat breathe again. The final ​-t is the feminine ending.

## Mythology

Serket is a guardian more than a protagonist: she appears wherever protection is most needed, arms outspread over the thing she shields. Her ​mythic presence clusters around the dying god — she is one of the four goddesses of the canopic equipment in the Osiris cycle — and around the threatened child, ‌above all the young Horus hidden in the Chemmis marshes.

### The Four Guardians of the Dead (Osiris Cycle)

When Isis wrapped the reassembled Osiris, the four great protective ​goddesses — Isis, Nephthys, Neith and Serket — took station at the corners of his bier and canopic chest. Serket’s scorpion stands for the poisoned threats of the night ‌that must be kept from the god’s body; her arms spread in the ‘Isis-knot’ gesture frame every royal sarcophagus hall.

### The Scorpion and the Child Horus (Metternich Stela)

The ​great cippi of Horus the child — the Metternich Stela above all — tell how the infant god was stung by a scorpion in the marshes and revived ‌by the divine mother's magic. Serket stands within that cycle as the power over the venom itself: the sting belongs to her, and so, therefore, does its antidote.

### The ​Scorpion of the King (Royal Protection)

From the earliest dynasties the scorpion guarded the king’s name — King Scorpion of the Predynastic period took the animal as his ‌emblem — and Serket’s image walked at the prow and stern of the royal barque. Her presence converts the desert’s deadliest small killer into a bodyguard.

### She Who Waits ​at the Head of the Bier (Funerary Texts)

In the tomb, Serket and her three sisters stand at the four sides of the sarcophagus, each uttering protection: ‘I am ‌Serket, I encircle with my protection.’ Her protection is specifically against poison and bite — the everyday killers of the Nile valley made powerless at the moment of ​greatest vulnerability.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Srqt concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Mistress of Poison** — ​Commander of the scorpion’s sting; her priests were the healers of venom bites.
- **Guardian of the Dead** — One of the four goddesses protecting the canopic chest and ‌the sarcophagus itself.
- **Protector of Children** — Her amulets warded nurseries; the scorpion on a wall meant “no venom enters here”.
- **The Breathing Throat** — Her name is a ‌cure: she who lets the constricted throat of the stung breathe again.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Srqt survives in a small number of securely identified remains, ‌catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

She stands at the corners of Tutankhamun’s canopic shrine ​— the gilded goddesses of the treasury are among the most photographed objects of Egypt — and in relief on royal sarcophagi from the Old Kingdom onward. Her scorpion ​emblem marks protective amulets by the thousand in museum collections.

## Realm & Domain

**Srqt** — Serket — is the scorpion’s sting turned to medicine: the goddess of venom and ‌its cure. She guards the vulnerable — children, the poisoned, the dead in their most helpless passage — and her scorpion crawls at the feet of kings and ​coffins alike, holding the poison at bay by its mere presence.

## Across Cultures

Serket was early fused ​with the greater scorpion-powers of the pantheon and by the New Kingdom is barely separable from Isis in her protective aspect; some temples give her a healing consort-form of ​Horus. The Greeks called her Selkis and kept her as a goddess of the dead; her name entered the magical papyri of late antiquity as a power-word against ‌poison.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[asklepios|Asklēpiós]], [[bhaisajyaguru|Bhaiṣajyaguru]], [[brigid|Brigid]], [[eir|Eir]], [[gula|Gula]], and [[hygieia|Hygíeia]], each linked through healing / medicine.

## Cultural Legacy

Her image — woman with ​a scorpion on her head, arms winged out in protection — is one of the most immediately readable Egyptian glyphs of care. The Metternich Stela and the Horus ‌cippi made her the patroness of a whole genre of healing magic that persisted into Coptic exorcistic texts.

Srqt is ​a name that performs its function: read it, and the throat opens. The scorpion-goddess guards this page as she guarded the bier — quietly, at the corners, with poison ​turned outward. Plain letters are her amulet: nothing decorative survives translation, but the protection does.
